Four complaints, one cause

The email that gets cut, the boxes that collide, the note that grows the row, and the badge that will not say which rows. Three of the four are the same fault — and it is not overflow. Every picture is the real platform, signed in, with addresses the length yours actually are.

The cause, in one number

The register is 1417px of table in a 1005px window

Eleven columns, and at 1280px the box that holds them is 1005px wide. So the table runs 412px past its own edge, every column is squeezed to §88’s 150px cap, and the two frozen columns — Name on the left, Save/Cancel on the right — float over whatever is underneath. That is not an overflow bug. It is a table that does not fit, and the four things you reported are what that looks like from four angles.

The two facts that decide it. Making the Email column wider on its own makes the register worse — 514px past the box instead of 412. And making the table fit on its own leaves all 33 addresses cut, because §88 caps every cell at 150px whether there is room or not. Neither works alone; together they do.

Option B — the reading side

Six columns by default, the rest one click away

Name, Unit, Email, Roles, Status, Password. Full Name, Job title, Official BU, Emp ID, Sign-in name and Mobile stay in the Columns chooser that already exists — nothing is removed, the default changes.

Nobody loses a column they chose. A stored preference wins over the default (§30.2), so this only changes the view for people who have never opened the chooser. The cost is that Job title and Official BU stop being on screen by default — which is the right trade if the register is read for who someone is and what they can do, and the wrong one if you reconcile against the employee file every day. Your call.

Option E — the editing side

The open row becomes a panel, not eleven little boxes

The register does two jobs: read 33 rows, edit one. A row is the wrong shape for the second — it is where a 158px cell has to hold an address, a role picker, a refusal sentence and a dropdown, and where the frozen column floats over your controls. Opening a row opens a panel underneath it instead. Every field below is the platform’s real control, moved — not a drawing.

What it reverses, stated. §79.2 made rows edit inline at your ask — “work on the row inline and then a small save button”. This is still inline and still that button; what changes is that the editor stops being confined to the row’s own cells. It also gives the two things we have been fighting a natural home: the role picker’s refusal sentence, and the note below.

The note that grows the row

“They said Retail Stores — Use it” becomes a mark

A sentence in a 150px cell takes a second line, so every row with a declaration is 57px against its neighbours’ 39px. That is exactly the wrapping §88 was written to end, arriving by a road §88 did not walk.

“I don’t know which lines to check”

The badge should land you on the rows, not on the page

The rail badge sums three counts — units with no custodian, people never issued a password, people who said where they work. Pressing it opens the register and stops there, which is why it tells you a number and leaves you to find it.

  • Pressing the badge applies the filter. The register already has filter chips (Active, Retired, No password, No email); two more finish the set — Said where they work and Duplicates — and the badge lands with one lit.
  • One count cannot be a row filter, and should say so. “3 units with no custodian” is about units, and this register lists people. It names the three units instead, and sends you to the row where you would give somebody the role.

This is §16.7’s rule applied to a notice rather than a refusal: a thing that tells you something is wrong has to be able to take you to it.

The rename

“BU owner”, and what it touches

Worth doing because it reads better in a chip — but it is not what fixes the width: measured, it buys 18px, because the Roles column is held open by Strategy custodian and the picker, not by Business unit owner.

The cost is real and small. The role name is written into the people workbook as a validation list and as an exported value, and the upload reads it back — so a file downloaded before the rename holds the old word. The reader has to take either (§58, §65: write the new label, read both). Supporting function head is the longer offender if you want the same treatment.

And the Add row — you are right, I had not counted it

Not one of its three fields sits under its own heading

It is one cell spanning nine columns with three boxes laid out inside it, so the column boundaries above it mean nothing. Measured at 1280px:

The fieldSits under
Full nameName · Full Name · Job title · Official BU
Emp IDOfficial BU · Unit
EmailUnit · Email · Roles · Status · Password · the actions column, which clips it

It needs no answer of its own. If the open row becomes a panel, then so does this: + Add someone opens the same panel with the fields empty. One editor shape for adding and for editing, the special-cased row disappears entirely, and the “already on the register” warning gets somewhere with room to be read.

If we do the small version instead, this row still has to be dealt with separately — and the only honest fix inside a table is to label the three boxes, since aligning them to columns that can be hidden puts the mapping back at the mercy of the Columns chooser.

What I would build

  • All of it, in this order: fewer default columns + the Email column allowed to hold an address; the open row and the Add row as one panel; the declaration note as a mark; the badge landing filtered; BU owner.
  • If you want the smallest change instead: fewer columns + Email only. That fixes the cut addresses and gets + role back down to 1280px, and leaves the panel for later — at the cost of the same collision returning on a laptop below that, and the Add row needing a fix of its own.

Tell me which, and whether Job title and Official BU should stay on by default — that is the one choice in here I should not make for you.
